analysis.one_liner: Taxes away most excess profits on rare-disease drugs that become blockbusters.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced by one sponsor with no cosponsors, it sat in the Ways and Means Committee until the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have imposed a 75% tax on the excess profits of "orphan drugs" — drugs for rare diseases that the government rewards with seven years of exclusive sales rights. The tax would apply only after a company had recovered its full development costs, and only on revenue above 125% of the drug's production and marketing costs [S3]. The idea was to claw back windfalls when a drug developed for a tiny patient group turns into a blockbuster seller.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, taxpayers would have recaptured part of the return on drugs developed with the help of federal incentives — market exclusivity and research credits under the Orphan Drug Act — when those drugs turned into blockbusters. Patients with rare diseases could have faced downward pressure on prices, since a 75% levy on profits above 125% of production and marketing costs gives a company little reason to price far beyond cost [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 75% tax on windfall profits from orphan drugs during their seven-year exclusivity period, applying only to revenue above 125% of the drug's production and marketing costs
Protects ordinary returns: the tax applies only after the company has fully recovered its development costs, and development costs are reduced by any federal funds received for the drug

Targets a specific imbalance: orphan drugs are developed for small patient populations with government-granted exclusivity, but some become highly profitable anyway; the bill's tax is designed to capture those excess returns

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, drug companies holding exclusive rights to rare-disease drugs would have paid 75% of windfall profits — the portion of sales revenue exceeding 125% of production and marketing costs, counted only after total development costs were recovered [S3]. Some of that cost could have been passed on to the small groups of patients who need these drugs [S3].

drawbacks.text: A 75% tax on profits above a set threshold could weaken the incentive to develop drugs for very small patient populations, since high prices during the exclusivity window are what make those investments worthwhile — the same exclusivity the bill taxes is the reward Congress created on purpose

The calculation is complex: the bill requires the government to determine allocable marketing costs, qualified clinical testing expenses, and federal funding offsets for each drug, opening the door to disputes over how to measure a 'windfall'

The tax applies only during the seven-year exclusivity period and only above 125% of production and marketing costs, so a company that delays recognizing revenue could reduce or defer much of the levy

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — reclaiming part of the excess returns on drugs developed with a government-granted monopoly — was real but narrow, touching a small set of very expensive rare-disease drugs rather than drug prices across the board. Its cost, acknowledged honestly by supporters, was the risk of dulling investment in drugs for tiny patient populations, where high expected profits are the main reason to invest at all. The design tried to manage that by exempting all profits up to full cost recovery, but the tax's complexity and the threat to research incentives gave opponents solid grounds to object.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and no committee ever voted on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the bill on April 1, 1993 and spoke for it on the House floor the same day and again on April 5
No other member signed on as a cosponsor
The House referred the bill to the Ways and Means Committee, which never considered it; the action history records no markup, no vote, and no further movement for the rest of the 103rd Congress
The bill expired when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Orphan drug manufacturers are better off: the windfall profits tax never came close to enactment, so exclusive rare-disease drug rights continue to produce unlimited profits free of any excess-profits levy. Taxpayers and rare-disease patients gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.role: Sponsor; member of the Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never scheduled a markup or floor vote

sides.party_line_note: No roll call was ever taken; the bill drew a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors, and the Democratic-led Ways and Means Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Companies holding seven-year exclusive rights to rare-disease drugs would have owed a 75% tax on profits above 125% of production and marketing costs once development costs were recovered [S3]. The bill died, so these manufacturers keep the full returns that exclusivity produces — profits that ultimately come from prices paid by patients and, through insurance, by everyone else.

The Orphan Drug Act pairs exclusivity with tax credits for clinical testing; this bill would have layered a windfall levy on top of those incentives without repealing them [S3]. The industry's core privilege — exclusive sales rights for rare-disease drugs — remained untouched.
